lines.text: About sixty-five billion neutrinos from the Sun pass through your little fingernail every second, and almost none of them touch anything. So how do you catch one?

lines.text: This year's Nobel Prize in Physics went to Francis Halzen, for decisive contributions to IceCube, a telescope made of Antarctic ice, and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos from space. Four steps, and three guesses for you.
lines.source_text: This year's Nobel Prize in Physics went to Francis Halzen, for decisive contributions to IceCube, a telescope made of Antarctic ice, and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos from space. Four steps, and three guesses for you.

lines.text: Step one: the ghost particle. Guess: a high-energy neutrino crosses a whole kilometre of ice. What are the odds it hits anything on the way?
lines.source_text: Step one: the ghost particle. Guess: a high-energy neutrino crosses a whole kilometre of ice. What are the odds it hits anything on the way?

lines.text: In our toy model, about one in sixty-five thousand. So the detector had to be huge.
lines.source_text: In our toy model, about one in sixty-five thousand. So the detector had to be huge.

lines.text: Step two: the telescope. In nineteen eighty-eight, Halzen and John Learned proposed using the ice itself. Halzen then led the team that built it.
lines.source_text: Step two: the telescope. In nineteen eighty-eight, Halzen and John Learned proposed using the ice itself. Halzen then led the team that built it.

lines.text: When one does hit, it makes a charged particle faster than light travels in ice. It leaves a cone of blue light, and each sensor times its arrival.
lines.source_text: When one does hit, it makes a charged particle faster than light travels in ice. It leaves a cone of blue light, and each sensor times its arrival.

lines.text: Step three: our toy telescope. From the light's timing alone, it finds the particle's direction. Neutrinos fly straight, so that points back to where they came from. Guess: same ice, strings twice as far apart, so a quarter as many. How much worse does it aim?
lines.source_text: Step three: our toy telescope. From the light's timing alone, it finds the particle's direction. Neutrinos fly straight, so that points back to where they came from. Guess: same ice, strings twice as far apart, so a quarter as many. How much worse does it aim?

lines.text: In our toy model, more than five times worse: fewer strings, less light. Trend only, not IceCube's real aim.
lines.source_text: In our toy model, more than five times worse: fewer strings, less light. Trend only, not IceCube's real aim.

lines.text: Step four: what it found. In twenty thirteen, IceCube reported the first evidence of high-energy neutrinos from outer space. In twenty sixteen, it caught this shower, replayed from the real data.
lines.source_text: Step four: what it found. In twenty thirteen, IceCube reported the first evidence of high-energy neutrinos from outer space. In twenty sixteen, it caught this shower, replayed from the real data.

lines.text: IceCube records about a hundred thousand neutrinos a year. Guess: how many of them come from outer space?
lines.source_text: IceCube records about a hundred thousand neutrinos a year. Guess: how many of them come from outer space?

lines.text: About a hundred, the Nobel Committee says. Most of the rest are made in our own atmosphere.
lines.source_text: About a hundred, the Nobel Committee says. Most of the rest are made in our own atmosphere.

lines.text: The prize honours that discovery: high-energy neutrinos from space. Which objects make them is still open: one nearby galaxy shows evidence, not yet proof.

lines.text: So how do you catch one? With a cubic kilometre of ice, still watching.
